content: The recommendations and conclusions were meticulously prepared by the IPC Global Unit team and subsequently distributed to the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members for their final approval or comments. All relevant suggestions and edits were incorporated into a second draft. This revised draft was then subjected to external peer review, and further modifications were made to address all pertinent feedback. The International Health Regulations (IHR) emphasize the critical role of infection prevention and control (IPC) as a central strategy for addressing public health threats of international concern. This has been demonstrated in recent outbreaks of infectious diseases such as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), and the Ebola virus disease outbreak in West Africa. These events underscore the importance of robust IPC strategies in mitigating the spread of infectious diseases. In light of these challenges, there is a pressing need to support Member States in developing and strengthening IPC capacities within resilient health systems. This need is driven by contextual and emerging factors in global public health, including the aftermath of the 2014 Ebola outbreak, the review of the IHR, and the implementation of the Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR). There is a global consensus that urgent action is required to prevent future epidemics and pandemics and to curb the spread of AMR. Four key issues highlight the necessity of strengthening IPC at both national and facility levels: 1. Post-Ebola Capacity Building: The Ebola outbreak prompted lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and all Member States to reassess their national and local approaches to IPC and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in healthcare facilities, with a focus on patient and healthcare worker safety. The WHO IPC Global Unit has identified a gap in evidence-based frameworks to support IPC capacity building at the country level. 2. Strengthening IHR Implementation: The IHR, which came into force in 2007, requires Member States to notify WHO of events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern. IPC practices at healthcare facilities are essential for containment during such events. Current monitoring and assessment tools for IHR core capacities strongly feature IPC, and it is anticipated that IPC will play a prominent role in the revised IHR evaluation framework. 3. Supporting the Global Action Plan on AMR: The 2015 Global Action Plan on AMR, endorsed at the Sixty-eighth World Health Assembly, mandates the development of national action plans by 2017. IPC is identified as one of the five strategic objectives to be included in these plans. 4. Core Components of IPC Programmes: IPC is fundamental to all health systems and directly impacts the health outcomes of patients and healthcare workers. Strengthened IPC capacity at national and local levels is essential for achieving integrated, high-quality, and people-centered health services and progressing toward universal health coverage. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) represent a significant global burden, particularly in LMICs, where high-risk populations such as ICU patients and neonates are disproportionately affected. The frequency of HAIs in LMICs is several times higher than in high-income countries, especially for device-associated infections. For example, ICU-acquired infections can affect up to one in three patients in LMICs. Surgical site infections (SSIs) are the most frequently reported HAIs in LMICs, with significantly higher risk levels compared to developed countries. The economic burden of HAIs is substantial, with estimates from the USA and Europe indicating multi-billion-dollar impacts. HAIs lead to increased hospital stays, unnecessary investigations and treatments, and additional time required for patient care. They also impose private costs on patients and caregivers, including out-of-pocket expenses and quality-of-life consequences such as pain, psychological trauma, and even death. Societal costs include lost productivity due to morbidity and mortality. Despite these challenges, the global burden of HAIs is likely underestimated due to gaps in surveillance and reporting systems. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further exacerbates the threat posed by HAIs. High levels of resistance to critical antibiotics, such as third-generation cephalosporins and carbapenems, have been reported for pathogens like Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. This resistance limits treatment options and increases reliance on last-resort antibiotics. The prevention and management of HAIs are therefore essential components of global efforts to combat AMR. Access to WASH in healthcare facilities remains alarmingly poor, with 38% of facilities lacking a water source and many lacking basic hand hygiene resources. This deficiency highlights the urgent need for improved infrastructure and IPC measures to ensure safe and effective healthcare delivery. In conclusion, HAIs pose a significant threat to the safety and effectiveness of health systems, prolonging hospital stays, increasing antimicrobial resistance, and imposing substantial financial and quality-of-life costs. While progress has been made in reducing HAIs, no country has completely eliminated the risk. Strengthening IPC programmes and addressing gaps in WASH services are critical to mitigating the global burden of HAIs and ensuring high-quality healthcare for all.
